10 units, each with key ideas, worked examples, a 10-mark exam-style question, common mistakes and quick recall

How this book matches your Diploma. The Diploma core has three parts, and every Diploma student completes all three:

  • Theory of Knowledge (TOK): at least 100 hours of teaching, assessed by an exhibition (internal) and an essay on a prescribed title (external);
  • the Extended Essay (EE): an independent research essay of up to 4000 words;
  • Creativity, Activity, Service (CAS): experiences and a project over about 18 months, with reflection. CAS is not given a grade, but it must be completed.

TOK and the EE are each graded A–E, and together they can add up to 3 points to your Diploma total (maximum 45 = 6 subjects × 7 + 3).

This book is about planning: how the core and your subject internal assessments (IAs) fit together over two years. The arithmetic in the examples was checked with Python. Always follow your school's calendar and the current IB guides. The mark allocations in the practice questions are our own guides, written in the style of IB markschemes.

Unit 1 of 10: The Diploma Core in One Page

Key ideas

  • TOK asks "How do we know?" It examines knowledge itself: the core theme knowledge and the knower, two of five optional themes (knowledge and technology, language, politics, religion, indigenous societies) and five areas of knowledge (history, the human sciences, the natural sciences, mathematics, the arts).
  • The EE is independent research. You choose a topic in a DP subject (or an interdisciplinary option), work with a supervisor, and write a structured argument of up to 4000 words.
  • CAS is experiential learning. You take part in creativity, activity and service experiences, complete at least one CAS project, and reflect on your growth against the seven learning outcomes.
  • They connect. TOK thinking improves the EE's evaluation; EE research skills improve your IAs; CAS reflection practises the honest self-assessment the EE reflection now rewards.

Worked examples

Example 1: a student studying Biology HL writes an EE on enzyme activity. The TOK question "How do we know a result is reliable?" feeds directly into the EE's discussion of uncertainty.

Example 2: a CAS service project tutoring younger students gives a real-life situation for a TOK exhibition on "knowledge and the knower".

Example 3: a History IA on source evaluation trains the same skills needed for EE Criterion D (discussion and evaluation).

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Name the three parts of the Diploma core and state how each is assessed. [6]

(b) Explain two ways the parts of the core support one another. [4]

Answers:

  • (a) TOK: exhibition (internal, 10 marks) and essay (external, 10 marks), graded A–E (A2). EE: an externally assessed essay of up to 4000 words, graded A–E (A2). CAS: not graded; completion is required for the Diploma (A2).
  • (b) TOK evaluation skills strengthen the EE's discussion of evidence (R2); CAS reflection builds the habits rewarded by EE reflection (R2).

Common mistakes

  1. Treating CAS as optional because it is not graded.
  2. Thinking TOK is "just philosophy" with no link to your subjects.
  3. Leaving the EE until the second year.
  4. Forgetting that TOK and the EE can add up to 3 points.
  5. Not using the same research habits across IAs and the EE.

Quick recall

  1. What is the EE word limit?
  2. How many optional TOK themes do you study?
  3. How many areas of knowledge are there?
  4. Is CAS graded?
  5. What is the maximum Diploma score?

Answers: 1) 4000 words. 2) Two. 3) Five. 4) No, but it must be completed. 5) 45.
